extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent practitioners, patent attorneys, and disciplinary counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria used in USPTO attorney-discipline proceedings assessing practitioner conduct (e.g., neglect, misrepresentation, certification obligations) and the factors used to determine sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner certification / reasonable inquiry (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.18(b), 11.18(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: By signing a document submitted to the US PTO, a practitioner certifies that he has conducted 'an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances' to ascertain that 'the claims and other legal contentions therein are warranted by existing law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to conduct such an investigation is a violation of the Disciplinary Rules (see 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(15)). The page criticizes relying on unchallenged assumptions (e.g., assuming an invention remained viable) as not constituting a reasonable inquiry. Examples: checking intervening prior art, contacting the inventor, reviewing one's own website for prior publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signing a paper filed in violation of § 11.18 (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(15))
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes signing a paper filed with the USPTO in violation of the provisions of 37 C.F.R. § 11.18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where a practitioner executed a submission while certifying a reasonable inquiry had been performed but no such inquiry was made. The document links this subsection to the certification obligation and treats it as a specific violation when certification is false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes neglect of a client's legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider prolonged inaction (e.g., a 20-month delay in filing, losing or forgetting a file) and inadequate docketing/filing systems as evidence of neglect. The page finds neglect where the practitioner misplaced a file, lacked safeguards to discover the loss, and failed to act once rediscovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly giving false or misleading information to the USPTO (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a),(b) via 10.23(c)(2)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits knowingly giving false or misleading information or knowingly participating in giving false or misleading information to the USPTO or its employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires proof that the practitioner knew the statement was false or misleading and intentionally provided it. The page explains that if the practitioner did not know a statute applied, the OED Director has not proven a knowing misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess whether actions (e.g., concealing information from a client or USPTO) were motivated by a desire to deceive. The Court found pervasive neglect but declined to find sufficient clear-and-convincing evidence of deceitful motive in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice—generally when conduct impacts negatively the public's perception or efficacy of the courts or legal profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts ask whether the practitioner's actions harm public confidence or the legal system. Neglect that harms a single client may reflect poorly on the individual but does not necessarily implicate the profession as a whole; thus, not every instance of neglect constitutes this violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly violating requirements of 37 C.F.R. §§ 1.56 or 1.555 (via 10.23(c)(10))
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes knowingly violating or causing to be violated the requirements of specified USPTO disclosure or practice provisions (cited as §§ 1.56 or 1.555 in the decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish this violation the OED must show the practitioner knew the law applied and nonetheless violated disclosure or related duties. If the practitioner lacked knowledge that a bar applied (e.g., 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)), the element of knowing violation is not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advancing claims or defenses unwarranted under existing law (37 C.F.R. § 10.85(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes knowingly advancing a claim or defense that is unwarranted under existing law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where a practitioner pursues positions without legal support. If the practitioner did not know the law barred the claim (because no inquiry was made), the element of knowing advancement is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealing or knowingly failing to disclose required information (37 C.F.R. § 10.85(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits concealing or knowingly failing to disclose information that the practitioner is required by law to reveal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires knowledge of the obligation and an intentional failure to disclose. The page holds that one cannot conceal what one does not know; absent knowledge, this violation is not proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-all: conduct reflecting adversely on practitioner's fitness (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad provision regulating conduct that does not fall under the immediately preceding subsections but which adversely reflects on fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted as non-duplicative: if conduct violates specific subsections (b)(1)-(b)(5) it should not be separately charged under (b)(6). The OED Director must allege conduct falling uniquely within (b)(6) to sustain that count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden / Standard of proof: clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49 and case law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney-discipline proceedings require proof by 'clear and convincing evidence' (37 C.F.R. § 11.49), a standard between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision summarizes authorities (Addington v. Texas; Black's Law Dictionary) explaining that clear and convincing requires evidence that produces 'a firm belief or conviction' and is 'reasonable and persuasive.' The Court applied this standard to determine whether deceit or intent was proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative defenses pleading and proof requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: To raise an affirmative defense in a USPTO attorney-discipline proceeding, the respondent must 'state affirmatively in the answer special matters of defense' and the statement must (1) specify the defense; (2) explain the defense's nexus to the alleged misconduct; and (3) explain the reason it provides a defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative defenses must be proven by clear and convincing evidence. Generic or unsupported assertions (e.g., 'failure to state a claim' without elaboration) are insufficient and will be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) and ABA Standards guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing sanctions, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty to client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether conduct was intentional, knowing, or negligent; (3) amount of actual or potential injury; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court often consults the ABA's Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for guidance on severity and on weighing aggravating/mitigating factors. The page applies these factors to weigh negligence versus intentional misconduct and to calibrate sanction severity (e.g., suspension/exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (examples and how they affect sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include extensive prior disciplinary history, repeated warnings, and failure to remedy systemic office-management problems; mitigating factors include long experience, successful prior practice, and returning fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior suspensions and multiple disciplinary investigations increase sanction severity. Returning client fees can mitigate but may be viewed as self-interested (timing matters). The Court weighs these facts contextually; experience can be aggravating (if it undermines excuse) or mitigating (if showing competence overall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office management and docketing obligations as a quality metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are expected to maintain adequate filing, docketing, and communication systems to prevent missed deadlines, lost files, and failures to transmit Office Actions/Notices of Abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inadequate systems (antiquated filing, lack of docket management, poor staff communication) are evidence of negligence and foreseeably lead to client harm. The decision treats systemic neglect as a factor supporting sanctions and recommends remedial overhaul of procedures to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counts aggregation rule (violation of 10.23(c) constitutes violation of 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c) constitutes a violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a), which proscribes engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural rule explains how specific subsection violations map to broader misconduct counts; it guides charging and disposition strategy in pleadings and findings.
